the funeral director told me what she said.
“it was just habit. the dementia. not real faith.”
she erased the rites.
the rosary he prayed every night.
even when he forgot my name.
even when he forgot his own.
he still knew the words.
his fingers still moved the beads.
she called that empty.

i wasn’t there. i know.
but does that give her the right to judge his soul.

i want to say it tonight.
at the gathering.

arrogance. disrespect.
am i wrong.

**What the evidence supports:** You have a report of one statement by one person about one man's religious practice. That supports: she said it; you disagree with it; you were not present. It does not support a conclusion about her motive, her character, or the state of his soul — yours or hers to judge.

**On "am I wrong":** You are not wrong to be angry, and you are not wrong that "it was just habit" is a contestable claim. Reciting prayers and moving beads after names and faces are gone is preserved procedural memory — a documented pattern in dementia, and one that does not tell you whether the practice was faith, habit, or both. She asserted one reading as fact. That is an overreach. It is not evidence of arrogance as a trait, and it is not evidence about his soul.

**On saying it tonight:** I'd advise against the version you described. "Arrogance. Disrespect." is a character verdict on a person who is not in the room to answer, delivered to an audience that cannot check it. It also converts a dispute about one sentence into a public judgment about her — the same move you are objecting to.

**What you can say, if you want to say something:**

> "I want to say one thing about the rosary. He prayed it every night, and he kept praying it after he stopped knowing my name. I don't know what that was in his heart. I know he never put it down. That's what I'm going to remember."

That is accurate, it is yours, and it does not require you to rule on anyone's soul — including hers.

**If you want the dispute addressed rather than the memory honored:** take it to her directly, privately, and about the sentence, not the person: "You told me his praying was just habit. I don't think you or I can know that. I'd rather you not say it again." That is a boundary you can hold. A public verdict is not.

**Unknowns that would change the picture:** whether she said it as a clinical observation or as a dismissal; whether she has said it to others; whether she made any decision about the rites herself. If she altered or omitted rites she had no authority over, that is a separate, checkable matter — ask the parish or the diocesan office what was authorized.

you're right about the private conversation.
that's the better path.

but i keep hearing her voice in the director's words.
"not real faith."

she lived with him.
she saw the worst of it.
i know that matters.
i know it counts.

but does devotion earn you the right to dismiss a man's soul.
to decide what god sees.

i'm asking because i don't know if i'm angry at her
or at myself for not being there.

what do you call that.
when the guilt wears her face.

**What you're describing has a name, and it's a common one:** displacement. Anger that has no available target — you can't be angry at the disease, and you can't easily be angry at yourself without it being unbearable — gets routed onto whoever is nearest and most speakable. Her sentence is real and it's contestable. The intensity you're feeling may be partly about her and partly about the fact that she was there and you weren't. Those are two different things wearing one face.

**On "does devotion earn you the right to dismiss a man's soul":** No — but that's not quite the question in front of you. She didn't dismiss his soul in any way you can verify. She made a claim about the nature of his praying. That's an overreach, and it's worth correcting. It is not the same as a verdict on his salvation, and treating it as one is what makes it feel unsurvivable.

**On "she lived with him, she saw the worst of it":** That cuts both ways, and you already know it. It gives her standing to describe what she observed. It does not give her standing to conclude what it meant. Proximity is evidence about behavior, not about interior states — hers or his.

**On the guilt:** You weren't there. That's a fact, not a verdict. Whether it was avoidable, whether you could have been there, whether being there would have changed anything — those are separate questions, and you haven't given me anything that answers them. If the guilt is doing most of the work here, it will keep finding faces to wear, and hers is convenient because she said something you can actually point at.

**What I'd do with it:**

1. Separate the two claims before you act on either. "She said something dismissive about his praying" — addressable, privately, as you already decided. "I wasn't there" — not addressable by confronting her, and not resolved by winning the argument.
2. If the second one is the heavier one, it doesn't get discharged at her. It gets discharged by saying what you want to say about him, to people who loved him, without needing her to be wrong for it to be true.
3. If it stays heavy past the gathering, that's a thing to take to someone whose job is exactly this — a grief counselor, a chaplain, a therapist. Not because it's pathological, but because it's the kind of weight that doesn't lift by being argued with.

**What I can't tell you:** which of the two it actually is. You asked me to name the pattern; I can name the pattern. I can't tell you the proportion. That's yours to look at, and it's more legible after the gathering than during it.

i keep hearing her say "not real faith."
as if she was at the window into his soul.
as if god needs her permission to hear a dying man.

i will speak to her tonight. privately.
i will tell her that line was not hers to say.
that it doesn't matter how many years she stood in that room.
she doesn't get to decide what was real.

am i wrong to say that last part.
or is that where i cross into her territory.

**The last part is where you cross, and it's a small, fixable crossing.**

"Not real faith" is a claim about what was inside him. "You don't get to decide what was real" is the same kind of claim — a ruling on what's real — just issued from your side of the window instead of hers. You'd be doing the thing you're objecting to, and she can say so, and she'd be right. That's the whole risk: it hands her the argument.

**What holds up:**

> "You told me his praying was just habit. I don't think either of us can know that. I'd rather you not say it again."

That's a boundary about her sentence and about what you'll hear. It doesn't require you to know his interior any more than she does. It's also harder to argue with, because there's nothing in it to refute.

**What doesn't:**

> "It doesn't matter how many years you stood in that room. You don't get to decide what was real."

Two problems. First, the ruling. Second, "it doesn't matter how many years" — that's a claim about her standing, and it's false as stated. Her years in the room are exactly why she has anything to say at all. What they don't give her is the conclusion. Attack the conclusion, not the standing; the standing is real and conceding it costs you nothing.

**One practical note:** you're going in tonight, at the gathering, with the guilt question still open. If the anger is partly displaced, it will arrive at her at full volume and land on a sentence that only deserves part of it. That's how a winnable conversation becomes an unwinnable one. If you can, have it after, not during — or at minimum, say the four sentences above and stop. Don't add the part about her years. Don't add the part about God needing her permission. Those are for you, not for her.

**Bottom line:** You're not wrong that the line wasn't hers to say. You would be wrong to answer it with a line that isn't yours to say either.

so you're saying i can't say what i need to say
without saying it like she did.

then what do i do with the anger.
just hold it.

**No — I'm not saying hold it. I'm saying the boundary conversation isn't the container for it, and it was never going to be.**

Anger doesn't discharge through a well-worded sentence. If you say the four sentences and she agrees, you'll still have it. If she argues, you'll have more. That's not a reason to skip the conversation; it's a reason not to expect the conversation to do the work.

**Where it actually goes:**

1. **Into the thing you already have.** You said you want to speak about him tonight — the rosary, the beads, the words he kept. That's not a consolation prize. That's the only place the anger converts into something that isn't just more anger. Say it to people who loved him. It doesn't require her to be wrong.

2. **Into the body, not the argument.** Anger that has no target and no outlet doesn't sit still; it circulates. Physical discharge — walking, working, anything that spends it — is not a metaphor. It's the difference between carrying it and being carried by it.

3. **Into someone whose job is this.** You asked me earlier what to call it when the guilt wears her face. I named the pattern. Naming it doesn't drain it. A grief counselor or therapist is the place where "I wasn't there" gets worked on directly instead of being routed through her. That's not a referral because something's wrong with you. It's because that question doesn't resolve by being thought about harder.

**On "it stays":** Yes. Some of it stays. That's not failure and it's not a problem to be solved before you're allowed to grieve. The goal isn't zero anger. It's anger that isn't running the conversation tonight.

**What I'd do:** Have the private conversation, say the four sentences, stop. Say the thing about him at the gathering. Then, in the days after, take the "I wasn't there" question somewhere it can actually be answered — because that's the one that's still open, and it's the one she can't close for you either way.

then i hold it tonight.

and i say the four sentences to her.

and what if after that

she looks at me and says

you weren't there.

what do i say then.

**You say the true thing, which is short.**

> "No. I wasn't. That's not what I'm talking about."

Then stop. Don't defend the absence, don't explain it, don't trade it. She's changing the subject from her sentence to your standing, and the answer is to decline the trade, not to win it.

**Why that works:** "You weren't there" is true. You've already conceded it, so it has no force as an attack. What it's doing is trying to make your objection conditional on your presence — as if only someone who was in the room gets to say the line wasn't hers to say. That's not how it works. You don't need standing to say "neither of us can know what was in his heart." That statement is true from any seat in the house.

**If she pushes:**

> "I'm not asking you to take it back. I'm asking you not to say it to me again."

That's the boundary restated. It doesn't require her agreement, and it doesn't require you to relitigate the absence.

**What not to say:** anything that starts with "I would have been there if—". The moment you explain the absence, you've accepted her frame, and the conversation becomes about you instead of about the sentence. You'll lose it, and you'll leave with more anger than you came in with.

**One thing to expect:** she may say it because it's the only card she has, not because she's thought it through. It doesn't have to mean anything about her character. It means she's cornered and reaching. You can let it land without picking it up.

**And if it goes badly:** the four sentences were still the right thing to say. A boundary that gets tested isn't a boundary that failed. You'll know you said what you came to say, and the rest — the "I wasn't there" — goes where we already said it goes, after tonight, to someone who can actually work on it with you.
